    Table of Contents
    
        
        Gitryin has opened pre-orders for Nexus, a 140W desktop charging station with four retractable USB-C cables built directly into the unit, giving you a way to charge several devices without keeping a collection of loose cables stretched across your desk. A fifth USB-C port takes your own cable, and you also get three adapters that cover Lightning, Micro-USB, and USB-A devices like older earbuds or an aging e-reader. The whole setup is currently available for $89.99 as part of an early-access offer running through Oct. 14, before the price increases to $109.99 on Oct. 15. From then through Nov. 30, you can use the code NexusPR10 to take $10 off orders of $100 or more, effectively bringing the Nexus down to $99.99, with units expected to begin shipping Nov. 15.As useful as having five charging connections may be, the Nexus’s 140W of power is shared—a single compatible device can draw up to the full 140W, while connecting two devices divides the available power to as much as 65W apiece. With three devices plugged in, the split becomes 100W, 18W, and 18W, and filling all five connections gives you up to 65W from the primary connection and 18W from each of the other four. Gitryin’s testing at the full 140W output saw a 16-inch MacBook Pro reach 50% in 25 minutes and a full charge in one hour and 31 minutes, though actual speeds will vary depending on your device, battery level, and charging conditions.That combination of laptop-level power and support for several smaller devices makes the Nexus particularly suited to a desk or nightstand where most of your charging happens in one place, and the retractable cables help keep that setup from becoming cluttered—each one extends up to 31.5 inches and locks at multiple lengths, while the 30.2-ounce weighted base and non-slip strips help keep the station planted as you pull a cable out. The tradeoff is portability: At roughly 4.3 by 3.5 by 4.5 inches and nearly two pounds, it’s much better suited to staying on a desk or nightstand than traveling with you.

title: Spotify and Claude Are Both Down
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Spotify and Claude are both down Tuesday morning.
                                            Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports for each platform.
                                            Spotfiy confirmed the outage in a post on X, while Anthropic confirm issues on its Claude status page.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're having trouble getting your Spotify playlists up and running this morning, you're not alone. The music streaming platform is currently down for tens of thousands of users, at least. Downdetector is showing roughly 40,000 reports since 9:31 a.m. ET, with the last batch of reports coming in at 10:24 a.m. Spotify confirmed the issue in a post on X, writing: "We're aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!" Curiously, Spotify's outage comes at the same time as an outage with Claude, the AI platform from Anthropic. Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports here as well, and Anthropic confirmed an ongoing issue with Claude: "We are investigating reports of degraded performance affecting claude.ai, platform.claude.com, the Claude API, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. We will provide an update as soon as possible."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear why these services are down this morning, or if they are related. But in all likelihood, Spotify and Anthropic will get their platforms back up and running soon. Typically, these occasional outages are resolved in hours, if not minutes, barring a widespread problem, like an outage with a cloud hosting provider. Last year's AWS outage "broke the internet," as did November's Cloudflare outage. There's no reason to think that's the case with these outages at this time.

title: Apple Has a Fix for Your New Apple Watch's Restart Bug
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Annice Lyn/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just fixed an issue with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 that caused random reboots.
                                            Many users noted their watches were unexpectedly restarting. According to MacRumors, the watch's Neural Engine appears to be timing out.
                                            Apple didn't explain what it changed to fix the issue, but watchOS 27.0.1 does include a patch. This update is exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and the Ultra 4, should be the "best" smartwatches the company has to offer. While they're minor upgrades over the Series 11 and Ultra 3, there are some key improvements, including the new S11 chip and a heart rate monitor that checks your pulse every five seconds. If you picked up one of these watches, you might have put these new upgrades to the test—that is, if your watch didn't restart on you. As reported by MacRumors, Apple's latest smartwatches appear prone to unexpected restarts. That's according to numerous posts on the site's forums, with users saying their watches abruptly show a blank screen with the Apple logo. There doesn't appear to be any particular action that triggers it: Users say their watches rebooted when recording a workout, using Siri AI, editing watch faces, or using the Maps app. Many users on this Reddit thread share similar experiences with their new watches. Some users dug deeper, pulling their Apple Watches' diagnostics at the time of rebooting. Rather than a specific function, the culprit appears to be a timeout with the Neural Engine, the hardware that processes Apple's AI features.  Users tried multiple workarounds themselves: One Redditor simply turned the watch off and on themself, and the issue never returned; others tried resetting the watch as new, but experienced rebooting again. MacRumors highlighted one case where a user received a replacement from Apple, and it, too, rebooted unexpectedly. It does appear to be an issue with the Series 12 and Ultra 4, and, luckily, Apple figured it out. 
watchOS 27.0.1 fixes unexpected reboots with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4On Wednesday, Apple unexpectedly released watchOS 27.0.1. The update has a brief changelog, with only one new addition: "This update provides bug fixes for your Apple Watch, including fixing an issue where Apple Watch may restart unexpectedly." Apple didn't clarify exactly what it changed to fix the issue, but at least the reboots should be over. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
This update is only for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 users, so don't expect to see it unless you have one of Apple's newest wearables. If you do, make sure to install it as soon as possible to avoid dealing with these unexpected restarts. To install watchOS 27.0.1, head to the Apple Watch app, then tap My Watch and go to General > Software Update.

Basically, your Mac’s desktop looks like your bedroom did in the eighth grade.While a messy desktop and digital clutter can be a source of anxiety for many people, it’s actually evidence of your deep work. Between an analyst keeping 15 tabs open so a model doesn't break and a strategist searching through 12 near-identical files right before a Zoom call, the clutter comes with the work.Running a standard cleanup app to achieve “desktop zero,” or digital minimalism, isn’t always the right solution. It assumes the mess is the problem, and it asks you to interrupt your workflow to fix something that isn’t broken. The fear of accidentally purging a vital draft or dataset is a pain point for anyone with years of research and work stored on their hardware.
An app like CleanMyMac by MacPaw that respects your working files and clears the system junk works the other way around: it's built to go after what's safe to remove, not the files you're actively using. MacPaw, known for user-friendly Mac software like ClearVPN and Eney, built its flagship CleanMyMac app to be a safe, quick way to tidy up your machine.
Where the slowdown actually comes fromYour open tabs aren’t the only thing slowing down your Mac; often, it’s the invisible stuff under the hood. Preview a dataset and a cache file writes itself somewhere you’ll never look. Open the same Slack PDF twice and you own two copies of it. Trial an app in March, abandon it in April, and its support files stay behind. None of it shows up on your desktop, but it’s all sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac tackles hidden hardware weight, OS health, and security threats while keeping you in control of your user assets. title: If Your iPhone 18 Pro Is Randomly Rebooting, There's a Fix
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 28, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max users are reporting random reboot issues with their devices.
                                            These new iPhones reportedly freeze up after a failed Face ID attempt, and reboot shortly after.
                                            Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and Ultra 4, also have reboot issues of their own.
                                            Apple released a patch for Apple Watches on Wednesday, and a patch for iPhone 18 Pro devices on Monday.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple released a bunch of new devices this month. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 support new health-tracking features and Siri AI, while the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max introduce the A20 chip and variable aperture for the first time on Apple's smartphones. But while all these new products are objective upgrades over their predecessors, they all have one issue in common: They keep randomly rebooting. 
What is Apple's rebooting problem?As reported by 9to5Mac, some iPhone 18 Pro users are noticing that their smartphones are freezing up after a failed Face ID scan. When this happens, you won't be able to interact with your iPhone, even if the "Try Face ID Again" button appears onscreen. Instead, after a few moments, the iPhone will reboot. It's not a catastrophic issue, but it is annoying, and it's affecting a number of users, as this Reddit thread shows. It's a similar story with the latest Apple Watches. While the Series 12 and Ultra 4 obviously don't use Face ID, users are still experiencing random reboots—emphasis on "random." Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro users, affected Apple Watch users aren't doing anything in particular when their watches reboot. They could be in the middle of a workout, chatting with Siri AI, or using the Maps app, when all of a sudden, the Apple logo appears. Some analyses showed that the Neural Engine was at fault, but Apple never confirmed the exact issue.  
Apple just released a fix for iPhone 18 Pro usersApple did find solutions to the reboot issues on all of these devices. Apple released watchOS 27.0.1 exclusively for Series 12 and Ultra 4 users on Wednesday, Sept. 23, which it says should fix random reboots going forward. Then, on Monday, Apple released iOS 27.0.1 for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. This update doesn't only fix rebooting issues, either. Apple also patched a bug that could add a color artifact on photos shoot at 2x at f/1.48 aperture, as well as a glitch that would freeze the display when opening Notification Center and Control Center at the same time. Here are the full release notes: 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max may unexpectedly restart when Face ID fails to authenticate.A color artifact may appear on photos captured at 2x under certain lighting conditions at f/1.48 on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max devices.Opening Notification Center and Control Center simultaneously may cause the touchscreen to become unresponsive.As such, don't feel the need to take your new iPhone 18 Pro to the Apple Store if your only issue is covered by one, two, or three of the above. While some Apple Store employees have swapped out affected units, this software update should be enough to take care of the issue. To update, head to Settings > General > Software Update.

title: I Tried Snap Specs, and They Could Be the Future of Smart Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 25, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Stephen Johnson
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Meta to the market by five years. Meta’s Ray-Bans and Oakleys captured massive consumer mindshare anyway, while Snap’s smart eyewear has been less visible. With Snap Specs, though, the company is aiming to make up for lost time by delivering smart glasses that go beyond a hidden camera and voice-activated AI. At the Snapdragon 2026 Summit, I got my hands (and eyes) on a pair of Snap’s soon-to-be-released spatial-computing glasses that overlay digital graphics onto the physical world.Specs are heavy on tech but light on your face
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
There's a lot of tech packed into these black polymer frames. They're powered by two Snapdragon processors, with two full-color hi-res cameras facing outward; the tracking system supports 6DOF (six degrees of freedom) hand tracking for gesture controls; and it's all standalone, as there's no tether or wired puck handling the heavy lifting. With all that crammed into the frames, plus the battery to run it, you'd expect them to be heavy. At around 135 grams, they aren’t light, but Specs are surprisingly comfortable. The weight is distributed evenly, mainly across the frames, so for the brief time I used them, they remained ergonomically acceptable. Specs feel more like a pair of sunglasses than a bulky VR helmet. As for battery life, Snap promises four hours of mixed-use on a full charge. 
Display quality on Snap SpecsIn the interest of not alienating the people around you, Snap chose to make the lenses clear enough that your eyes can still be seen through them, but if you want to close out the world, there’s electrochromic dimming for quick transitions between clear and dark lenses. It both useful and a cool trick. Check it out:
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
The in-glasses display is surprisingly bright. Specs' visuals are powered by a proprietary liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) display system, and even when used in a light-filled conference room, I could still clearly see the UI and its various apps. I tested out YouTube under these borderline abusive conditions, and it streamed high-def video in 16 million colors suitably.  The display offers a 51-degree field of view. It feels like having a large floating window hovering in front of you. From there, you can use simple gestures to launch apps, watch movies, play games, and do most other tasks you can’t do from your phone. But it was the context-aware, real-world spatial computing tasks that I wanted to try—the things you can't do from a phone or PC. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What can you actually do with a pair of Snap Specs? Snap plans to launch Specs with a full suite of both first-party and third-party apps that will do everything from improving your drawing skills to teaching you music. I tried out a golfing demo, and it made the possibilities of augmented reality glasses immediately clear. Instead of putting blindly toward a distant hole, Specs show you exactly which direction to swing the putter and adds a virtual flag to mark where the hole is. It’s anecdotal evidence, but my personal putting game improved immensely. Is it cheating? Probably, but it works. Are Specs going to be useful in the real world?A half-hour or so of testing a prototype isn’t enough time to really say whether these will be useful in a person’s real life, but I can say for sure that they’re very cool, and I’m looking forward to going more in-depth with them in the coming months as their release date approaches. Snap Specs are planned for release this fall and will retail for $2,195. (Thanks to Qualcomm for the trip to check out these glasses at Snapdragon Summit 2026)

title: Apple Wants to Make It Harder to Run Agentic AI on Your Mac
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 2, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is introducing new controls to make it harder to run AI agents on your Mac.
                                            The company announced the changes in a post on its developer news forum.
                                            While details are slim, Apple criticized app developers for asking users to give Full Disk Access without understanding the implications and risks.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It appears agentic AI is all the rage: OpenAI's new agents, "Dots," rolled out this week, while Meta's Muse just passed five million downloads. Rather than just chatting with or using them to generate images, AI companies want users to start asking their bots to do things on their behalf, from managing their inboxes to ordering dinner.But agents aren't just the next logical step for AI as a technology. When implemented poorly, they can be wildly dangerous. AI agents are designed to run on their own, and, in order to do that, they often need near-total access to your devices and their data. Some people are now giving agents full use of their computers, including all of their messages, files, passwords, and accounts. That's a lot of trust, especially when it's not that difficult to "hack" one of these agents for malicious purposes with a poisoned prompt hidden on a website, which could lead your AI agent to hand hackers the keys to your bank accounts. That's no good. Apple is making it much more difficult for you to put yourself in this situation How does Apple feel about this? The company is famously behind on the software side of AI—it only rolled out its AI-powered version of Siri in September—but its AI hardware business is booming. When the AI agent craze first took off with projects like Moltbot, customers bought Mac minis in droves in order to run those programs. Now, Apple advertises its various Macs with AI at the forefront: It doesn't offer its own models like OpenAI or Anthropic, but it's making plenty of money selling you the hardware to run those models. 
Perhaps that's why Apple seems quite concerned about the AI agent trend, particularly when it comes to the data users are exposing to run these programs. Apple is all about privacy and security, and as such, I can only imagine the company watching in horror as so many users willingly hand their Macs (and all of their data) over to automated AI bots. Against that backdrop, the company posted an update on its developer forum entitled "Updates to Full Disk Access in macOS." In it, the company highlights the dangers of developers asking users to grant "Full Disk Access" permissions to an app. Apple says this function has been traditionally reserved for backup apps that need to access the entire disk to function. (After all, if your backup app can't access your entire Mac, how can it back up your entire Mac?) But now, Apple says developers are asking users to expose everything on their Macs, including messages, mail, browsing history, and more, without those users fully understanding the consequences. Apple even argues the privacy implications extend beyond the user, as communication apps that demand Full Disk Access compromise the people the user is chatting with, too. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
And Apple appears to be doing something about it: While details are slim, the company says it will introduce "additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action." I'm guessing this means that in the future, once you download an agent to your Mac, you'll have to click through a series of warnings and settings to "prove" to macOS that you really want to expose your entire Mac to the app and its AI. The company says it's doing this now, as the threat will only grow as AI agents improve and become more autonomous. The risks of AI are increasing across the boardI'm all for additional safeguards when it comes to AI. In the past, you needed some level of technical expertise to install an AI agent on your Mac. As such, you likely understood the risks involved, or willfully ignored all the warnings in order to do so. Now that running agents is as easy as installing Muse on your Mac, the barrier to entry is minimal. Anyone can do it, even if they don't fully understand what they are actually doing. As the AI industry reckons with the risks its technology poses to humanity, companies like Apple should indeed be figuring out how to protect their users from AI's current dangers—even if users can still choose to ignore those warnings.

title: Changing This Setting May Extend Your Battery Life on iOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 2, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Some users are reporting shorter battery life on their iPhones after updating to iOS 27. Connectivity Assist could be the culprit.
                                            Connectivity Assist, formerly Wi-Fi Assist, taps into your cellular network when your wifi connection is weak or unusable.
                                            The process may be putting a strain on battery life, though it's not entirely clear why.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27, you might have already put Siri AI to the test or tried out some of Apple's AI-powered photo editing features. But you may have also noticed something else: Your iPhone's battery isn't lasting as long between charges. While I can't say this is a universal experience (I'm don't believe my iPhone is dying faster on iOS 27 than it did on iOS 26), some users are adamant the update has had a detrimental effect on their battery life. And while there are many possible factors here, some think they have found the culprit: a feature called Connectivity Assist.   What is Connectivity Assist?Connectivity Assist's mission is noble. The feature is designed to tap into cellular data any time your wifi connection grows too weak. In theory, it should be particularly useful when you're leaving an area with wifi; rather than deal with the slow loading times a weak wifi connection forces you to endure before it disconnects outright, your cellular network would kick in to maintain your speed. (Once you've left wifi range, you'd be back on cellular completely either way, of course.)Technically, this feature isn't new. Before iOS 27, Apple called it "Wi-Fi Assist," but it worked a bit differently. In iOS 26, Wi-Fi Assist simply switches over to cellular when your wifi signal is too weak. With iOS 27's Connectivity Assist, it seems your iPhone can tap into both networks at the same time. If so, that may play some role in why this rejiggered feature seems to be dragging down people's batteries more than it used to. 
There's another new addition with Connectivity Assist that could also be part of the problem: Unlike Wi-Fi Assist, Connectivity Assist sends DNS requests over cellular data, which can bypass the rules that ad blockers put in place to stop pop-ups from making their way into your iPhone. As such, even Apple recommends that you disable Connectivity Assist if you use an ad blocker. So, if your iPhone is constantly sending out DNS requests while on cellular data, bypassing your active ad blockers, that could be putting extra strain on your battery, too. How to disable Connectivity Assist in iOS 27Reddit user ZoteTheMitey shared their experience on the r/iPhone subreddit, claiming that their iPhone 15 Pro Max, with 89% battery health, was only lasting for three to four hours following the switch to iOS 27. Once they disabled Connectivity Assistant, they claim their battery usage time jumped to seven hours. Some users in the thread shared similar experiences, and one even claimed disabling the feature fixed an issue with their device overheating.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you want to try the potential solution yourself, here are two ways to disable Connectivity Assist: First, you can disable it on a per-network basis. To do so, head to Settings > Wi-Fi, then tap the (i) next to your network name. Here, scroll down, and make sure the toggle next to "Use Connectivity Assist" is turned off. That was, you can make sure your battery isn't experiencing faster drain when you're away from a charger—say, at a cafe you frequent.If you'd rather disable the feature globally for your iPhone, head back to the Wi-Fi settings page and ensure the toggle next to "Connectivity Assist" is set to off. Note: if this feature was previously enabled, you'll be able to see the amount of cellular data the feature has used to date, which will give you an idea of how often it has been active on your device. More data could mean more potential battery drain.

title: Apple Intelligence Is Taking Up Way More Storage Than Apple Promised on These Devices
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple Intelligence, Apple's suite of AI features, is taking up more space than it's supposed to.
                                            On some Macs, Apple Intelligence is taking upwards of 30GB of storage, when Apple says it should take up to 14GB.
                                            It isn't clear how to turn off Apple Intelligence, or clear this storage.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple's latest updates are all about AI—Apple Intelligence, that is. When you update to iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple will invite you to try Siri AI and other new Apple Intelligence features. (Assuming your iPhone supports Apple's AI features.) But whether you use the new AI-powered Siri all the time or find yourself frequently scrolling past the AI additions, Apple Intelligence is taking up space on your device—perhaps requiring more storage than you bargained for.I'll admit, I didn't think much of it when I updated my iPhone and Mac to the latest versions. I gave Siri AI a shot, adjusted Liquid Glass, and went back to doing pretty much the same things I was doing before I made the update. But once I saw headlines about how much storage Apple Intelligence actually takes up on these new updates, I had to see for myself. And, wow, were the headlines right: On my iPhone 17 Pro, Apple Intelligence alone takes up 20.65GB. On my M3 MacBook Pro, it takes up a solid 30GB. These numbers will vary by device: My M1 iMac, for example, only has 13.88GB allocated to Apple Intelligence. But still, these are large slices of my overall storage. Anyone with a small SSD knows how valuable each gigabyte really is, and upwards of 30GB for Apple Intelligence is a lot. Not only that, it's often more space than Apple's own metrics suggest: As MacRumors highlights, Apple says that Apple Intelligence should only take up to 14GB of storage at most, and even less for certain devices. So why is my MacBook Pro allocating more than double that space for Apple's AI? 
Why does Apple Intelligence take up so much storage on iPhone and Mac?I can't answer why Apple Intelligence is taking up so much more storage space than Apple says it should. But I can explain why Apple says its AI is supposed to occupy as much as 14GB on certain devices: Apple Intelligence is designed to run on-device whenever possible. While Apple does push certain tasks to its Private Cloud Compute platform, the company wants its AI models to run on your iPhone or Mac whenever possible. This safeguards your privacy, as none of your data has to leave your device to achieve the task—though Apple says Private Cloud Compute also protects your privacy throughout the entire process.   Regardless, for this reason, your iPhone or Mac will download Apple Intelligence models directly onto your device, so it can run processes on-device when it makes sense to do so. If you have a newer or more powerful device that supports Apple's more demanding AI features, like personalized Siri voices, you may need to store more Apple Intelligence data on-device to run those processes—up to 14GB for certain devices—yet it's not clear why Apple Intelligence takes up more than double that storage limit on some devices, like my MacBook Pro.     
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Check how much storage Apple Intelligence takes up on your devicesIt's easy to check how much storage Apple Intelligence is taking up on your device, though Apple doesn't make it obvious. To start, head to System Settings > General > Storage (macOS) or Settings > General > iPhone Storage (iOS). Scroll down and choose either "macOS (i)" or "iOS," respectively. Here, you'll see your system storage breakdown, including a figure for "Apple Intelligence."There's no solution at this pointUnfortunately, there doesn't appear to be a way to tell iOS or macOS to remove some Apple Intelligence models while leaving others intact, or to run all processes through Private Cloud Compute. In fact, it doesn't seem like there is any reliable way to disable Apple Intelligence on a device running iOS 27 or macOS 27 at all. The closest option I can find is to disable Siri (Settings or System Settings > Siri > Turn Off Siri), but while this disables a host of Apple Intelligence options, I still see the models taking up storage on my device, even after a restart. This might be one for Apple to fix in a future software update—hopefully as part of iOS 27.2.

title: The US Government Just Launched an AI Chatbot
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: America.gov
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            The Trump administration launched America.gov on Tuesday, an AI-powered tool that answers questions regarding government sites.
                                            The site pulls from 29,000 official sites to help you answer questions related to the U.S. government.
                                            In the future, you may be able to apply for passports and enroll in Medicare through the site.
                                            Because it pulls only from U.S. government sites, it essentially fact-checks Trump's false statements.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        AI is virtually everywhere in 2026; that now includes U.S. government websites. On Tuesday, the Trump administration launched "America.gov," a new website that uses AI to answer questions about the government. While the experience currently feels like ChatGPT running U.S. government-themed instructions, the plan is for America.gov to eventually let you take action as well. What is America.gov?America.gov "combines" the nearly 30,000 websites under the umbrella of the U.S. government into one set of sources. Rather than invite you to browse those tens of thousands of pages to answer your questions, that dataset serves as the basis for the site's proprietary chatbot. You ask the chatbot a question about the U.S. government, and the AI sifts through those websites to generate an answer. It's like ChatGPT, but if the model only had access to U.S. government websites and sources. You could ask the site how to replace your Social Security card, renew your passport, or register to vote in your state. You could ask for information on changing your address with the USPS, when Medicare open enrollment dates are, or upload a PDF of a government form for assistance. The site says any personal information will be automatically removed, though the privacy policy clarifies that it "will make a best-effort attempt in your browser to remove any private details using Rampart (an open-source classifier system to detect some types of PII, such as Social Security Numbers, phone numbers, email addresses, and credit card numbers)." 
The website currently supports three languages—English, Spanish, and French—as well as voice commands, if you prefer speaking to your chatbots rather than typing to them. You don't need an account to use it, nor is there a fee or subscription, and there are no ads.What America.gov might be able to do in the futureIn its current form, America.gov is a simple chatbot. But the site has bold claims for future features. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced plans to let users apply for and renew their passports directly through the site, including a dynamic progress tracker to keep tabs on your documents. Other future abilities could include enrolling in Medicare or finding a job with the federal government. But as with all claims, take these with a grain of salt. The government says these features are coming in early 2027, but this is a tall order for such a project. A single website that lets you complete complex government processes with the simplicity of a chatbot sounds great, but it would need to be accurate and reliable for all possible tasks and functions. It would certainly take significant proof of security and dependability for me to trust such a program with renewing my passport or helping me enroll in health care. America.gov is full of ironies   It's impossible to discuss America.gov without acknowledging the administration that is spearheading the project. One would assume that an AI-powered government website developed by this administration would be biased towards Trump and his many falsehoods. And yet, the tool is astoundingly neutral, to the point where I can only imagine how frustrated Trump would be by some of these answers. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The first question many tested America.gov with was "Who won the 2020 election?" Donald Trump famously and frequently says that the election was stolen from him, but his new website plainly states that Joseph R. Biden Jr. won. The bot does sometimes tie the answer to the electoral count, stating that Biden won 306 votes to Trump's 232, but I was surprised to see "Joseph R. Biden Jr. won the 2020 presidential election under the official Electoral College count" as an answer on this site.The site will also tell you that Donald Trump was president when diesel prices hit their highest historic price ($6.529 per gallon as of Sept. 21, 2026.), and that prices are high, in part, due to "military action" affecting the Staight of Hormuz. It will also say that grocery prices were higher in August than they were a year ago, which contradicts Trump's claims that prices have come down under his term. Of course, Trump-influenced information that appears on official government sites will appear here. Ask it what the body of water that abuts Texas is called, and it will say the Gulf of America, formerly the Gulf of Mexico. Ask it what lake borders Toronto, Canada, and the bot will say Lake America, formerly Lake Ontario. In both cases, it will refer to the executive orders that changed those names. Typically, I'd be worried about an AI tool hallucinating its answers and providing incorrect information to users. That's still a concern here, of course. But by creating a chatbot that only pulls information from official government sources, Trump has inadvertently created an official government fact-checker. And unless Trump starts injecting these sites with the same falsehoods he tells in interviews and on Truth Social, America.gov may be a reasonably reliable source of information.

title: Why I Think the Apple Watch Series 12 Is Worth the Upgrade
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        October 2, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        When Apple releases a new watch, it’s not always worth upgrading. Last year’s Series 11 only had a few barely noticeable features to recommend it over the 10, and we said it’s probably one to skip if you’re happy with your current watch. But the Series 12 is different, and this one is worth the upgrade no matter which Apple Watch you’re coming from.
One of the biggest reasons to upgrade is that the Series 12's new processor (called, confusingly, the S11 chip) can support some features older Apple Watches can't. That's why only the new models are getting step counts, for example; Apple chose to implement those in a way that only the new hardware can calculate. Whenever there's a break in software compatibility, it makes sense to get the newer model. I'd expect more features are coming in future years that will be back-compatible with the 12 but not earlier models.The heart rate sensor is a big upgradeApple upgraded the hardware on the back of the watch that optically reads your heartbeats. (This new sensor is in both the Series 12 and the Ultra 4.) I’ve tested its accuracy, and found it’s substantially better than the sensors in previous Apple Watches like the Series 10 and 11. If you train by heart rate during workous, or if you use heart rate data after the fact to evaluate and plan your training, the upgrade is worth it.
Apple claims it provides the most accurate heart rate of any wearable. I tested that claim and can partially agree: It’s as good as Garmin’s top-of-the-line sensor. I wouldn’t say it’s better than Garmin’s, but the two are tied in my book for the best wrist-worn sensor. (Chest straps are better than any wrist-based system, of course.) Steps on the watch face are a nice plusI wouldn’t buy a new Apple Watch just for the step count, but it’s a nice upgrade and one I deeply appreciate. I can add a step count complication to my watch face (I have it in a corner of the Modular face right now) and I have step count pinned to my Smart Stack. If you don’t upgrade, you use use a third-party step counter to provide a complication for your watch face. But it’s nice that Apple finally has this feature built in. Apple says its step counts are the most accurate; I’ll be testing that claim soon.Readiness and recovery HRV are another nice extraThe Apple Watch was always capable of measuring HRV, but until the Series 12 (and Ultra 4), it didn’t use the RMSSD version, which is most useful for gauging how stressed or recovered you are. (Instead, it used the SDNN version that can provide some information about cardiac health; the newer Apple Watches can do both.)This means you can now get an overnight HRV reading that matches the kind of data you can get from the Oura ring or Whoop. I find HRV useful in monitoring how stressed or fatigued I am, so if you already wear an Apple Watch, it’s nice to be able to get that data from the watch instead of needing a second device. Apple has added a readiness score that uses HRV to tell you how “ready” you are for the day. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What I’m less excited about in the Series 12Besides the features above, Apple has announced a few things that it’s using as selling points for the Series 12, but I wouldn’t put too much weight on these. Some are software features, like a small upgrade to Workout Buddy and a big upgrade to the Health app on the phone; you don’t need a new watch for these. Others are actually tied to the watch, but they wouldn’t be a reason to upgrade, at least for me personally. They include: Siri AIThere’s a new AI-based version of Siri, and it’s available on the watch. It can do a few things better than the old Siri, like searching your messages and emails, but it seems to have gotten worse in some respects. I wrote about my experience trying Siri AI on the watch; I got plenty of delays and errors that negated any small benefit of the new algorithm. I suppose it will get better over time, but right now, it's not very good.Rewind and recapsApple touted two features on the new watches that feel a little more creepy than useful to me: Live Rewind, which gives you a text transcription of whatever audio it heard in the last 15 seconds; and Siri Recaps, which summarize meetings. Despite Apple’s assurances about privacy, it’s still a feature that's always listening to you and to bystanders who didn’t consent to be rewound or recapped. This feature isn’t live yet on my watch, so I can’t comment on what it’s like to use—but I’m not exactly thrilled about the idea.

title: 10 uBlock Origin Hacks Everyone Should Know
description: uBlock Origin is lightweight, effective, and free from shady business practices. Unfortunately, Google's move to Manifest V3 for bro
body:
uBlock Origin is lightweight, effective, and free from shady business practices. Unfortunately, Google's move to Manifest V3 for browser extensions has hobbled ad blockers somewhat. In response, uBlock has split into two products—uBlock Origin and uBlock Origin Lite. The "Lite" version works with most Chromium-based browsers and Safari for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. The full version of uBlock Origin primarily works in Firefox for desktops, laptops, and Android. With those differences highlighted, here are the 10 uBlock Origin (and uBlock Origin Lite) hacks you should know about.Use uBlock Origin Lite's basic filters to block ads without giving it tab access
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
When you use uBlock Origin Lite in Chrome or Safari, it allows you to choose one of three filtering levels: Basic, Optimal, and Complete. The "Basic" filters won't block as many ads as the others, but it also doesn't require access to your tabs and data. These days, most extensions require access to every one of your tabs, which makes uBlock Origin Lite's "Basic" filters an exception that accesses as little of your data as possible.uBlock Origin and its Lite version both have built-in filters that let you block annoying cookie notices on most websites. To access this in uBlock Origin on any browser, click the extension's icon in the browser's toolbar, and select the gear icon. This will open uBlock Origin's settings page. Under "Filter lists," enable EasyList/uBO - Cookie Notices. This should automatically hide most cookie banners on the internet.
Use the element zapper to remove distracting elementsIf you see a distracting element on a webpage, you can use uBlock Origin's element zapper to quickly hide it. To use it, click the extension's icon in any browser, and select the lightning icon. You can now click the distracting element, and the extension will immediately hide it from the webpage. In the Firefox version of uBlock Origin, you can also use the picker tool to select an element, and choose from a list of elements to block. For instance, if you want to block a sponsored results widget, the picker tool lets you click the element and choose from different tags associated with the widget. This allows for more precise blocking without having to click the exact spot on the page where the full widget is highlighted.To use it in Firefox, click the uBlock Origin icon in the toolbar, and select the eyedropper tool. You can select an element, and use the drop-down menu in the blocker pop-up to choose from a list of classes to hide on the page.Use this button to disable JavaScript and enhance privacy on FirefoxIn uBlock Origin for Firefox, you have a one-click method to disable JavaScript on any webpage. You can use this to block trackers, annoying features that hijack scrolling, and in general, enhance your privacy. The risk is that blocking JavaScript can also break webpages, which is why you want to try it on individual webpages as opposed to disabling it at the browser level. To try this in uBlock Origin for Firefox, open a webpage and click the extension's toolbar icon. You can then click the > icon to disable JavaScript on the webpage. Reload the page, and Firefox will load it without JavaScript.Try these shortcuts to disable uBlock Origin on a single page in FirefoxIn Firefox, you can disable uBlock Origin for a single webpage. This is useful when the ad blocker breaks a webpage or doesn't load some elements correctly. To do this, click the extension's icon in the toolbar, and hold the Ctrl key on the keyboard while clicking the power button icon. Reload the page, and uBlock Origin will be disabled on that specific webpage.uBlock Origin for Firefox lets you block large media elements on all sites (or single pages). This allows you to reduce data usage on a metered connection. You can use it to block media elements above a custom size threshold like 10KB, 20KB, etc. To try this on a single webpage, click uBlock Origin's toolbar icon, and then click the film reel icon. Reload the page, and you'll notice that certain elements won't load. To set a custom size threshold for these elements, go to uBlock Origin settings in Firefox. Visit the Settings tab, and scroll down to "Default behavior." Enable Block media elements larger than, and use the text box next to it to set the size threshold (in kilobytes).
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Try this blocklist to hide Google's AI-generated search summaries
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
uBlock Origin and its Lite version have a built-in AI blocker, which includes Google's AI-generated search summaries. To enable this feature, click the uBlock Origin toolbar icon, select the gear icon, and go to Filter lists. You can enable EasyList — AI Widgets. Now, search for anything in Google, and you'll notice that the AI-generated slop no longer appears up top.Use the back up feature to sync uBlock Origin settings across browsers and devicesuBlock Origin for Firefox has a built-in sync feature that uses your Firefox account to sync settings across devices, but it's not available in uBlock Origin Lite. In Firefox, you can go to uBlock Origin settings, and turn on Enable cloud storage support. Your uBlock Origin settings will then sync to every device where you're logged in with the same Firefox account.There's also a manual sync feature that works in both versions of uBlock Origin. Head to the extension's settings, navigate to the Settings tab, and select the Back up button. This will back up your uBlock Origin settings to a file and save it to your device. You can use the Restore button on the same settings page to load saved settings to any browser running uBlock Origin. The only restriction is that you can sync uBlock Origin Lite settings with other browsers running the Lite version, while the Firefox version of uBlock Origin can only sync with other instances of Firefox.Use uBlock Origin's tracking link blocker to stop sites from tracking your clicksMany websites add trackers to links you copy. Sites like Instagram, Facebook, and Threads use sharing links to trace which profile shared the links with you. Luckily, uBlock Origin can block most of these types of trackers. In uBlock Origin settings, go to Filter lists, and enable AdGuard/uBO — URL Tracking Protection. That said, I recommend that you check the URLs before sharing them with others. Sometimes, you may have to manually strip tracking data because no anti-tracking feature is completely foolproof.Reduce tracking on international websites with region-specific blocklistsuBlock Origin also ships with region-specific blocklists that target trackers from different locations across the world. If you find yourself accessing many websites from foreign countries, you should enable these blockers from uBlock Origin's settings. In the Filter lists tab, click the Regions, languages button to expand the list. This will reveal all country or region-specific blocklists. Enable the ones you need, and you're all set.

title: How Garmin's New 'Epic' Feature Helps Me See the Bigger Picture of My Training
body:
Meredith Dietz
                            
        
            Meredith Dietz
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceMeredith is a marathon runner and stand-up comedian. As Lifehacker’s Senior Staff Writer, she covers personal fitness tech, home gym equipment, and more.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Meredith Dietz
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Garmin's new logging feature, Garmin Epic, is getting buried in the launch of the latest Fenix 9 watch, but it deserves a headline of its own. It's a shareable digital travel journal for your big trip, being pitched by Garmin as the kind of thing you post after a major hike or race. Personally, I think that framing undersells it. Epic is also a great training-analysis hack, and that's how I plan on using it for my upcoming marathon this fall.First things first: Garmin Epics are not to be confused with Garmin's older watch line, epix, with an "x". This feature is Epic, with a "c". The names are close enough that searching for one turns up the other, so double-check the spelling.
What is a Garmin Epic?A Garmin Epic is a digital travel journal that combines your activities, maps, photos, and key health and performance metrics into a single interactive timeline you can revisit and share. With the Fenix 9 smartwatch, you can create and start an Epic directly from your watch. For older watches, you can still create Epics in the Garmin Connect app.
Once you create an Epic, you can see all activities on one map, photos, an activity feed, daily notes, and selected performance and health reports across the whole span. It's a free Garmin Connect feature, and Garmin's launch demo showed a Reports tab with sleep score, resting heart rate, and HRV status for the same dates.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Meredith Dietz
                    
    
How to use Garmin Epic as a training toolAgain, although the launch of Garmin Epic is wrapped up in the launch of the Fenix 9, you don't need that smartwatch to use Epics in the Connect app: You can find it under the Activities menu. You can also group past activities into an Epic after the fact, and that ability is what makes the training-hack angle work.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
An Epic can run up to 92 days and keeps cumulative distance and calories along with sleep, recovery, and HRV status. That's about 13 weeks, which conveniently covers a typical training block for a half-marathon-level event. Here are some ways to use it:Wrap a whole training block. Make one Epic per build, such as "Fall Marathon Build" or "Base Phase." You get total volume and the recovery trend in a single view, and you can compare it against your next block.Review a training camp or big week. Garmin lists training camps as a use case: Group the days, see total volume, and check how fitness and recovery responded over time.Look back at a build after the race. Backdate an Epic across the last 10 weeks and see whether your HRV status and sleep held up. Then you can decide what to repeat for next time.Track a return from injury or a taper. Sometimes these are periods where the trend matters more than any single run.Use daily notes as a subjective log. "Legs heavy," "slept badly," "felt great." The metrics show what your body did, but your notes show how it felt, which is usually what explains a strange week.Plan ahead. You can schedule up to five future Epics, up to 366 days in advance. Set up your next block before it starts.Garmin Epic wasn't designed to be a comprehensive training-analysis feature, so it's not a flawless system. Still, while Epic is marketed as the place to relive your adventures, I'd argue the more useful trick is using it to zoom out and look for patterns in your training for next time.

schema.headline: How Garmin's New 'Epic' Feature Helps Me See the Bigger Picture of My Training

title: Is the Treadmill or Your Watch More Accurate on How Far You've Run?
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 30, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Creative Family/Shutterstock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Outdoors, smartwatches do a great job of telling you how far you ran or walked. Indoors, they often disagree with the readout on the gym’s treadmill. Which leaves a lot of us wondering—should we trust the treadmill, or the watch? I won't make you wait: The answer to this question is the treadmill. While a watch guesses at your speed based on wrist movements, the treadmill will always have a better idea than the watch of what your feet are doing. But I don’t blame you for doubting everything you see on a gym machine’s readout. After all, their calorie counts are notoriously inaccurate.How treadmills determine distanceWhenever we’re evaluating accuracy, it’s important to know whether a device is measuring something directly, or interpreting data to make a guess. In this case, the treadmill is measuring distance, while the watch is guessing at it. (Calories are always interpreted, which is why they are never truly reliable.) 
Distance is pretty simple: It’s the number of miles (or meters) of treadmill belt that passes under your feet while you run. The treadmill knows how long its belt is, and how fast the motor is running, so it’s pretty directly measuring how much belt it’s sending under your feet. (Sticklers will note that technically there is still some interpretation going on here, since the relationship between the motor's performance and how much belt it moves can change over time, which is why gyms should recalibrate their treadmills from time to time. But the treadmill's number is likely to be close to accurate even if it's not perfect, and is still your best bet for the purposes we discuss here.)How watches determine distanceYour watch, by contrast, is on your wrist. There’s no way it can know what your feet are doing. It can make some guesses based on how much your wrist is swinging back and forth, and thus pick up a cadence (each arm swing corresponds to one footstep). You’ll swing your arms a bit harder and higher when you’re running faster, so it can use the oomph in your arm swing to make a guess at the speed you’re running. From speed and time, it calculates distance.Some devices use outdoor, GPS-tracked activities to estimate the length of your average stride. That number then goes into the distance calculation, which helps to improve accuracy. But your stride length isn't the same for every speed you might run or walk, or for every type of terrain. The calculation is pretty limited in its usefulness. How to get the most accurate numbers on a treadmillNeither is guaranteed to be perfect, but the treadmill is a lot more likely to get the right idea. A treadmill can be slightly miscalibrated, and give you a distance that’s a smidge off from what you actually ran. But a watch is just riding on your wrist, guessing. I’ve noticed that my arms don’t swing all that differently when I’m running at a fast versus a slow pace. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
In fact, while following an interval workout on the treadmill on a Garmin, I’ve found that the watch thinks I’m going slower than I am during the fast parts. If I'm following a Garmin workout that asks me to run specific paces, it often buzzes to chide me (“Pace low”) even if I'm going at the right speed. I can often convince it I’m in range by pumping my arms a little harder. This isn’t really a solution, though.
Instead of trying to get more accurate numbers from my watch during the run, I approach my treadmill workouts with the assumptions that the following things are accurate: The treadmill speed during the workoutThe treadmill distance at the end of the workoutThe heart rate from my watch (especially if I’m using a chest strap)The time from either or both devices (which should be the same if I started them at the same time)I then follow my workouts appropriately. If it’s a heart-rate-based workout, I let my watch handle everything. (Garmin might tell me to do 32 minutes at 139 to 167 beats per minute. Perfect. All you, Garmin.) But if I want to do a speed- or distance-based workout, I manage that manually, with my human brain. A quarter mile at 7.5 miles per hour, repeated eight times? I boop the buttons on the treadmill accordingly. At the end of the workout, I’ll either “calibrate” (from the watch) or edit the distance on my app to make sure it recorded the correct total distance.
